title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
wiki_lead:
The Fall of the Berlin Wall and the fortified inner German border occurred after a Politburo press conference on 9 November 1989 prematurely announced that East Germans could travel without restrictions after, in the decades before, hundreds had been killed by Border Troops of the German Democratic Republic when trying to sneak through the Iron Curtain. 
Soon, people gathered at Berlin border crossings, citing the news that were broadcast in East and West, and puzzled border guards eventually let them pass in the late evening hours, with live television broadcasting worldwide. The next days, thousands travelled across the border, also in other places less covered by press. After this symbolic fall, obstacles were removed, former crossings were opened again, and following demolition, L-shaped concrete segments of the Berlin wall were actually falling and spread around the world.
In the early stages of the Revolutions of 1989, Hungary removed the fence in May and opened its border in August, and after many East German families had fled into the West German embassy in Prague, the CSSR followed in late September. Despite holiday season being over, East Germans continued to defect via neighbouring Communist Bloc countries, putting pressure on the East German leaders to either shut down these borders, too, or "letting steam off" by allowing disgruntled citizens to directly emigrate to West Germany. Long-term leader Erich Honecker was ousted in October, and while new communist leaders discussed a travel law, the premature publication led to a total loss of control over the formerly fortified, lethal border, and due to the ensuing Peaceful Revolution, over the country itself. After the first free elections in spring 1990 showed preference for a German reunification and for the Western Deutsche Mark. The DM already came in July, unification took place on 3 October 1990 when 5 new states joined the 10 old states of the Federal Republic of Germany, with reunited Berlin being a 16th state. Soviet occupation forces left in 1994.

Background


Opening of the Iron Curtain

The June 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre had shown what could happen under communist rule. The opening of the Iron Curtain between Austria and Hungary at the Pan-European Picnic on 19 August 1989 set in motion a peaceful chain reaction, at the end of which there was no longer an East Germany and the Eastern Bloc had disintegrated.  
After the picnic, which was based on an idea by Otto von Habsburg to test the reaction of the USSR and Mikhail Gorbachev to an opening of the border, tens of thousands of media-informed East Germans set off for Hungary. Erich Honecker dictated to the Daily Mirror for the Pan-European Picnic: "Habsburg distributed leaflets far into Poland, on which the East German holidaymakers were invited to a picnic. grok_lead: The Fall of the Berlin Wall refers to the events of November 9, 1989, when East German authorities, amid mounting domestic pressure, announced revised travel regulations that were interpreted as permitting immediate free passage to the West, prompting crowds to overwhelm border checkpoints and initiate the barrier's de facto collapse. The announcement stemmed from a press conference by Politburo member GÃ¼nter Schabowski, who, reading unvetted notes, stated that new exit rules would take effect "immediately," without immediate clarification, leading border guards to open crossings after hours of impasse. Erected on August 13, 1961, by the German Democratic Republic (GDR) to stem mass emigrationâover 3.5 million had fled to West Germany by thenâthe Wall symbolized the Iron Curtain's division of Europe, with its fortified "death strip" claiming at least 140 lives of attempted escapees under shoot-to-kill orders. The Wall's fall marked the culmination of the Peaceful Revolution in East Germany, driven by widespread protests in cities like Leipzig and economic stagnation that exposed the GDR's centrally planned system's inefficiencies, including chronic shortages, technological lag, and foreign debt exceeding $20 billion by 1989. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's policies of perestroika and glasnost, combined with his explicit refusal to intervene militarily as in prior suppressions (e.g., Hungary 1956, Czechoslovakia 1968), removed the external prop for the GDR regime, while Western pressures, including U.S. President Ronald Reagan's 1987 demand to "tear down this wall," underscored ideological contrasts in prosperity. By early 1990, systematic demolition began, paving the way for German reunification on October 3, 1990, and accelerating the Soviet bloc's dissolution. Though often portrayed as an accidental triumph of spontaneous democracy, the event's deeper causality lay in socialism's empirical failures: East Germany's per capita GDP trailed West Germany's by a factor of three, with productivity crippled by state monopolies and incentive distortions, rendering the Wall's purposeâcontaining a failing economy's exodusâultimately untenable without perpetual coercion. Mainstream narratives, shaped by post-event academic and media lenses prone to emphasizing elite missteps over systemic rot, underplay how the GDR's collapse validated market-oriented reforms' superiority in generating wealth and freedom, as evidenced by the rapid integration's challenges and East Germany's subsequent catch-up, albeit incomplete.
